summary: Ethiopia routes virtually every nationality through its official eVisa portal (evisa.gov.et) — a 30- or 90-day tourist eVisa approved before travel — with only Kenyan and Djiboutian passport holders entering visa-free under bilateral agreements.

Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate is required if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Vaccination is also widely recommended for travel outside Addis Ababa.

source.name: Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not a formal entry requirement, but medical facilities outside Addis Ababa are very limited — comprehensive coverage including medical evacuation is strongly recommended.

source.name: Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

onwardTicket.text: An onward ticket is not routinely demanded from eVisa holders, but airlines may ask for one at check-in — carrying proof of return travel is sensible.

source.name: Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; immigration officers may ask visitors to show means of support for their stay.

source.name: Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

currencyLimits.text: Foreign currency above roughly USD 3,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival, and Ethiopian birr may not be brought in or taken out beyond token amounts — currency rules change often, so keep exchange receipts and confirm before travel.

source.name: Ethiopian eVisa — Immigration and Citizenship Service

notes: Drones may not be brought into Ethiopia without prior authorization from the civil aviation authority — undeclared drones are confiscated at the airport.
Exchange money only through banks and licensed bureaux and keep the receipts — street exchange is illegal.

payments.text: Cards are accepted at major hotels and a growing number of venues in Addis Ababa, but Ethiopia remains overwhelmingly a cash economy — carry birr outside the capital and expect ATMs to be unreliable up-country.

safety.text: Addis Ababa and the main tourist circuits are generally calm, but armed conflict and inter-communal violence persist in parts of Amhara, Oromia and areas near the Tigray and Eritrean borders. Check current government travel advice, avoid the affected regions and land borders, and fly rather than drive between cities where possible.

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to March is the dry season — clear skies for the Simien Mountains, Lalibela and the historic north; the main rains fall from June to September.

idp.text: Ethiopia is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

driving.text: Ethiopia is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Ethiopia yet.

tips.text: Security conditions vary sharply by region — parts of Amhara, Oromia and areas near the Tigray and Eritrean borders remain affected by conflict. Check your government's travel advice shortly before departure and stick to the areas it considers safe.
Apply only at evisa.gov.et — lookalike third-party sites charge large markups. Visas on arrival are no longer reliably issued, so have the approved eVisa in hand before boarding.
Addis Ababa sits at about 2,355 m and the northern highlands are higher still — take it easy for the first day or two and drink plenty of water.
Ethiopia uses its own calendar (seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one) and counts the hours from dawn — always confirm whether a time or date is "Ethiopian" or "European" when booking.
Change money only at banks and licensed bureaux and keep every receipt — you will need them to convert leftover birr back, and unofficial exchange can land you in serious trouble.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Ethiopia?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes. Ethiopia requires nearly every nationality to hold a visa, and the standard route for tourists is the official eVisa at evisa.gov.et, approved before travel. Only Kenyan and Djiboutian citizens enter visa-free under bilateral agreements.

faq.question: How do I get the Ethiopian eVisa?
faq.answer: Apply online at evisa.gov.et with a passport scan and a photo. The single-entry tourist eVisa comes in 30-day (about USD 82) and 90-day (about USD 202) versions and is normally approved within one to three working days. Print the approval letter and carry it with your passport.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Ethiopia?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Ethiopia has shifted to the eVisa system and visas on arrival at Addis Ababa Bole Airport are no longer guaranteed, even for nationalities that once qualified. Apply online before travel.

faq.question: Is Ethiopia safe to visit?
faq.answer: Addis Ababa and the main tourist circuits are generally calm, but armed conflict continues in parts of Amhara and Oromia, and several governments advise against travel to specific regions. Check current travel advice, avoid land borders, and use internal flights rather than long road journeys where possible.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Ethiopia?
faq.answer: A certificate is only demanded if you arrive from a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. Vaccination is nonetheless widely recommended for travel outside Addis Ababa, along with routine travel vaccines — check with a travel clinic.
